description: We are a team of engineering students specializing in Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence, passionate about using AI, data and technology to solve real-world challenges. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to combine creativity, teamwork and technical skills to build an innovative and impactful solution. Our strengths include AI & Machine Learning, data analysis, coding, software development and data visualization.
summary:
THE THIRD EYE, developed by Team Parallax Zero, is an interactive platform designed to make satellite fire data more accessible, meaningful, and easier to explore.

We wanted to go beyond a conventional data dashboard and create an experience that connects scientific analysis with human understanding. Our project brings together three complementary elements.
Interactive Exploration allows users to investigate historical fire activity through maps, calendars, and visual trends. Scientific Evidence focuses on transparency, showing how observations are harmonized while making uncertainty, missing data, and the limits of each comparison clear. Storytelling brings these ideas to life through engaging visuals and simple narratives, making the experience accessible even to people without a scientific background.

To support this approach, we developed an interactive web prototype, a scientific processing and calibration pipeline, and structured data models. We have also carried out initial experiments using real satellite observations, while continuing to integrate the scientific results into the full exploration experience.

With THE THIRD EYE, we want people to do more than look at satellite data. We want them to explore it, question it, and understand the evidence behind what they see.
details:
THE THIRD EYE

Beyond Detection. Towards Understanding.

01 — OUR VISION

What if exploring satellite data could feel as engaging as discovering a story, while still being grounded in scientific evidence?

That question guided us throughout the development of THE THIRD EYE.

We didn't want to build another dashboard filled with charts and technical information. We wanted visitors to explore the data, understand how comparisons are made, and recognize the limits of what satellite observations can tell us.

Our approach brings together three elements: storytelling, interactive exploration, and scientific evidence.

02 — WHAT WE BUILT


A. RESEARCH LAB — Explore the Observations

The Research Lab is designed to turn historical satellite observations into an experience users can investigate themselves.

Its interface includes geographical exploration, satellite selection, historical calendars, charts, and comparison panels.

We developed these components to allow visitors to explore fire observations from different perspectives and understand how recorded activity varies across regions and time.

An important part of our design is distinguishing between actual observations, missing information, and results that cannot yet support a reliable comparison.

The interface has been developed, while the complete integration of historical data into all exploration features remains ongoing.

B. SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE — Understand the Results

We believe a useful visualization should also explain how its conclusions were reached.

Our scientific component processes MODIS and VIIRS observations, calculates observation-based fire-detection rates, and evaluates calibration methods intended to make the two records more comparable.

We also test different calibration variants, examine the sensitivity of the results, and document limitations.

This work is supported by real satellite observations, structured scientific data, and automated validation tests.

Rather than presenting every comparison as a definitive answer, THE THIRD EYE is designed to show where the evidence is strong, where uncertainty remains, and where a conclusion cannot yet be justified.

C. STORY MODE — Discover the Science

We created an interactive storytelling experience that introduces the science behind satellite observations.

Through 3D scenes, animations, and guided explanations, visitors discover how MODIS and VIIRS observe fire activity and why differences between their measurements matter.

Rather than beginning with technical formulas, we use visual examples to explain concepts such as sensor sensitivity, observation coverage, and misleading historical trends.

The goal is to make the scientific ideas approachable, even for someone discovering satellite data for the first time.

03 — HOW THE SYSTEM WORKS

Our architecture follows five main stages.

1. NASA Data Acquisition

We use daily fire observation products from Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS, with Google Earth Engine supporting the data processing workflow.

2. Data Preparation

The processing pipeline applies observation-quality filters, identifies active-fire pixels, and tracks usable observations.

Missing measurements are treated differently from valid observations with no detected fire.

3. Harmonization

We calculate fire-detection rates relative to usable observation coverage and estimate calibration factors to support comparisons between the two satellite records.

4. Scientific Validation

We evaluate calibration variants, examine errors, and record conditions in which the available evidence is insufficient.

5. Interactive Visualization

Scientific results are organized into structured data files that the web application can read and present through its exploration and evidence interfaces.

This separation between scientific processing and presentation helps keep the displayed information traceable to its source.

04 — OUR SCIENTIFIC WORK

Our initial real-data calibration experiments focus on California and British Columbia.

We used observations from 2016–2018 to estimate calibration factors and evaluated their behaviour on separate 2019 development data.

For California, the raw VIIRS rate showed a relative error of approximately −29.6% against the Aqua reference rate. After calibration, the error was approximately +3.7%.

For British Columbia, the corresponding error changed from approximately −26.4% to +14.5%.

These results demonstrate the effect of calibration in our development experiments. They do not establish that the method will perform equally well across every location or time period.

We also implemented checks for missing observations, insufficient data coverage, and sensitivity to calibration choices.

Our approach is built around a principle we consider essential: uncertainty should be visible, not hidden.

05 — TECHNOLOGIES AND TOOLS

Frontend Development
React, TypeScript, and Vite.

3D Experience and Animation
Three.js, React Three Fiber, GSAP, and interactive visual components.

Scientific Computing
Python and NumPy for data preparation, observation-rate calculations, and calibration experiments.

Data Validation
Pydantic, structured data contracts, and automated testing.

Satellite Data
NASA Aqua MODIS, Suomi NPP VIIRS, and Google Earth Engine.

Deployment
Vercel for the web application.

06 — WHAT MAKES THE THIRD EYE DIFFERENT?

Our project connects three perspectives that are often presented separately.

Scientific analysis helps us understand how satellite records can be compared.

Interactive exploration allows users to investigate observations rather than simply reading fixed conclusions.

Storytelling gives visitors a more natural introduction to complex scientific ideas.

We also designed the platform around transparency. Missing data, failed checks, and uncertainty are not treated as details to hide.

We want visitors to understand not only what the data shows, but also what it cannot establish.

07 — BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

For students and educators: An accessible way to introduce satellite observations and scientific data interpretation.

For researchers and data enthusiasts: An interactive environment for examining historical records, calibration approaches, and supporting evidence.

For the general public: An opportunity to understand how satellite measurements contribute to our knowledge of environmental change.

Our ambition is to make scientific exploration more accessible while encouraging a critical understanding of the information being presented.

08 — CURRENT PROGRESS AND LIMITATIONS

During the hackathon, our team developed the frontend experience, scientific processing modules, real-data calibration experiments, structured data models, and evidence visualization components.

We have not completed every feature we originally envisioned. In particular, full historical data integration and independent final evaluation remain important next steps.

We believe being transparent about this progress is part of presenting the project responsibly.

TECHNOLOGIES AND IMPLEMENTATION

THE THIRD EYE combines scientific data processing with interactive web development.

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and GSAP for the user interface, interactive scenes, and animations.

Scientific Processing: Python and NumPy for data preparation, observation-rate calculations, and sensor calibration.

Data Validation: Pydantic, structured data contracts, and automated tests to keep scientific results consistent.

Data Sources: NASA Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS daily fire products, processed using Google Earth Engine.

Deployment: Vercel for the browser-based application.

Our scientific calculations are performed separately from the frontend. The website reads prepared data and evidence files rather than recalculating the analysis in the browser.

HOW TO EXPLORE THE THIRD EYE

THE THIRD EYE is a browser-based experience. No installation or account is required to explore the published application.

1. Enter the Experience: Open our website and discover the main interface.

2. Follow the Story: Choose Story Mode to explore the scientific ideas through interactive scenes, visual explanations, and guided chapters.

3. Visit the Research Lab: Open the Lab to examine the available scientific evidence and calibration results. Historical calendars and regional exploration features are being integrated, so some sections may not yet contain data.

4. Examine the Evidence: Explore the calibration results and their limitations to understand how comparisons are assessed.

The project can be accessed from a web browser on a computer or compatible mobile device.

Live Project: https://the-third-eye-six.vercel.app/
